items.prompt: "All cats are reptiles. Fido is a cat. Therefore Fido is a reptile." Every premise here is false. What can we say about the argument's validity?
choices: It's invalid, because false premises always make an argument invalid
It's valid — the conclusion necessarily follows from the premises, regardless of whether the premises are actually true
Validity can't be assessed without knowing the premises are true
It's both valid and sound, since the structure is correct
items.explanation: Validity is purely structural: if you grant the premises, does the conclusion have to follow? Here it does, so the argument is valid — just not sound, because a premise (all cats are reptiles) is false. Validity and truth-of-premises are independent axes.

items.prompt: "If the build fails, CI blocks the merge. The build failed. Therefore CI blocks the merge." What pattern is this, and is it valid?
choices: Affirming the consequent — invalid
Modus ponens — valid
Denying the antecedent — invalid
Modus tollens — valid
items.explanation: This is "if P then Q; P; therefore Q" — modus ponens, valid in every case regardless of what P and Q stand for.

items.prompt: "If the build fails, CI blocks the merge. CI blocked the merge. Therefore the build failed." What pattern is this, and is it valid?
choices: Modus ponens — valid
Affirming the consequent — invalid, because CI could block the merge for other reasons (failing lint, missing approval, etc.)
Modus tollens — valid
This is the same argument as "if the build fails, CI blocks the merge; the build failed; therefore CI blocks the merge"
items.explanation: This affirms the consequent: knowing the merge was blocked (Q) doesn't tell you the build specifically failed (P) — CI could block for unrelated reasons. It's structurally different from modus ponens even though it reuses the same "if P then Q" premise.

items.prompt: "If the deploy succeeded, the health check would pass. The health check did not pass. Therefore the deploy did not succeed." Is this valid?
choices: No — this denies the antecedent
Yes — this is modus tollens: if P guarantees Q, then not-Q guarantees not-P
No — you can't reason backward from an effect to a cause
Only valid if you also know the health check is reliable
items.explanation: This is "if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P" — modus tollens, valid for the same reason modus ponens is: if P always produces Q, then Q's absence rules out P entirely, since there'd be no way to have P without Q.

items.prompt: "Senior engineers write extensive tests" gets restated in a discussion as "writing extensive tests makes you a senior engineer." What's the best description of what happened?
choices: Nothing changed — these are just two ways of phrasing the same claim
The relationship was silently reversed, the same structural move as affirming the consequent, dressed as a definition rather than a formal if-then
This is a modus tollens transformation and is valid
This is only a problem if the original claim was already false
items.explanation: "If senior, then tests" got restated as "if tests, then senior" — swapping antecedent and consequent, the same invalid move as affirming the consequent, just expressed in ordinary language rather than explicit if-then form. This is exactly the kind of move informal logic exists to catch, since it rarely appears with formal notation attached.

items.prompt: Implement `isValid(premiseFn, conclusionFn)` for two boolean variables P and Q. It should brute-force all 4 combinations of {P, Q} and return `{ valid: true }` if there's no combination where the premise is true but the conclusion is false, or `{ valid: false, counterexample: { P, Q } }` for the first combination that breaks it. Both `premiseFn` and `conclusionFn` are functions that take `{ P, Q }` and return a boolean.

tests.description: modus ponens (if P then Q; P; therefore Q) is valid
tests.expr: expect(isValid((e) => (!e.P || e.Q) && e.P, (e) => e.Q)).toEqual({ valid: true })

tests.description: affirming the consequent (if P then Q; Q; therefore P) is invalid
affirming the consequent's counterexample has P false and Q true
tests.expr: expect(isValid((e) => (!e.P || e.Q) && e.Q, (e) => e.P).counterexample).toEqual({ P: false, Q: true })

tests.description: modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P) is valid

items.explanation: Validity is defined as "no case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails" — for a fixed, small number of boolean variables that's directly checkable by trying every combination, exactly what the loop does. This is the same brute-force idea behind the truth-table checker in L3, just scoped to two variables so it's easy to trace by hand.
